title: BSD 1 — Test
src: Acute Rheumatic Fever & Rheumatic Heart Disease

mcqs.q: Acute rheumatic fever is an immune-mediated disorder triggered by:
mcqs.explain: ARF follows a group A streptococcal upper-respiratory infection (pharyngitis) by 2–4 weeks.

mcqs.q: ARF typically begins how long after the streptococcal infection?
mcqs.explain: Clinical features start about 2–4 (up to 5) weeks after the streptococcal infection.

mcqs.q: The proposed mechanism of ARF is:
opts: Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and host tissue (e.g. cardiac myosin)
Direct bacterial invasion of the heart valves
mcqs.explain: An autoimmune reaction arises from molecular mimicry between streptococcal M proteins and host tissues such as cardiac myosin.

mcqs.q: ARF most commonly affects which age group?
mcqs.explain: ARF mostly affects children and adolescents aged 5–15; it is rare before 4 and uncommon after 18.

mcqs.q: The most common and earliest major manifestation of ARF is:
opts: Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints
mcqs.explain: Arthritis is the most common and earliest manifestation (92% of adults): a fleeting, migratory, asymmetrical polyarthritis of large joints.

mcqs.q: The arthritis of ARF is best treated with:
mcqs.explain: The arthritis subsides in 4–6 weeks without permanent damage and is treated with aspirin/NSAIDs; carditis is treated with corticosteroids.

mcqs.q: Carditis (pancarditis) in ARF is suggested by:
opts: New or changed heart murmurs, with chest pain and dyspnea
mcqs.explain: Carditis presents with new/changed murmurs (mitral/aortic), chest pain, dyspnea, edema and palpitations; it is diagnosed on echo and treated with corticosteroids.

mcqs.q: Sydenham's chorea is distinctive because it:
opts: Occurs late (≥6 months), with normal ESR/CRP/ASO, and disappears during sleep
mcqs.explain: Chorea appears 6+ months after infection (so inflammatory markers/ASO are normal), causes purposeless movements that disappear in sleep, and mostly affects girls.

mcqs.q: Subcutaneous nodules in ARF are typically found:
opts: Over extensor surfaces and bony prominences, signalling severe carditis
mcqs.explain: The painless, firm nodules occur over extensor surfaces and bony prominences and are associated with severe carditis.

mcqs.q: Erythema marginatum is a highly specific sign that:
opts: Is a transient pink rash on the trunk, almost never the face
Is an itchy scarring rash of the face
mcqs.explain: Erythema marginatum is a highly specific, transient, non-scarring, painless pink rash with raised edges on the trunk and proximal limbs — almost never the face.

mcqs.q: Which finding supports recent streptococcal infection in ARF?
mcqs.explain: A high ASOT (>200 U/mL) and a positive throat culture for group A strep are evidence of recent streptococcal infection.

mcqs.q: The characteristic ECG abnormality in ARF is:
mcqs.explain: The ECG in ARF may show a prolonged PR interval (a minor Jones criterion).

mcqs.q: Diagnosis of ARF by the Jones criteria requires:
opts: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus evidence of streptococcal infection
A positive blood culture for staphylococcus
mcqs.explain: Jones criteria: two major, or one major plus two minor, together with evidence of recent streptococcal infection.

mcqs.q: For long-term secondary prophylaxis against recurrent ARF, the standard regimen is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units IM every 3–4 weeks
A single dose of oral amoxicillin
mcqs.explain: Secondary prophylaxis is benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2M units IM every 3–4 weeks, continued until age 20 (or ≥10 years after the latest attack).

mcqs.q: Which valves are predominantly damaged in chronic rheumatic heart disease?
mcqs.explain: Chronic RHD predominantly affects the mitral and aortic valves; the tricuspid is rarely and the pulmonary almost never involved.

mcqs.q: The most common complication of rheumatic mitral stenosis is:
mcqs.explain: Atrial fibrillation is the most common complication of mitral stenosis, and predisposes to systemic embolisation.

mcqs.q: Severe mitral stenosis is defined when the valve orifice is reduced to about:
mcqs.explain: Severe mitral stenosis is present when the normal orifice area is reduced to about 1 cm².

mcqs.q: Why is regular dental care emphasised in patients with RHD?
opts: Some procedures cause bacteraemia, risking infective endocarditis
Dental care cures the valve disease
It replaces the need for penicillin prophylaxis
RHD patients cannot have any dental treatment
mcqs.explain: Certain dental procedures cause bacteraemia that can seed damaged valves, so good oral hygiene and care reduce the risk of infective endocarditis.

mcqs.q: Most patients with RHD are anticoagulated, so dental treatment should be:
opts: Done under LA in consultation with the physician
Done after stopping all medication without advice
mcqs.explain: Because most RHD patients are anticoagulated, dental treatment is done under local anaesthesia in consultation with the physician.

mcqs.q: Conscious sedation with nitrous oxide for an RHD patient is acceptable when:
opts: Cardiac function is good and the physician approves
The patient is in heart failure
mcqs.explain: Nitrous-oxide conscious sedation may be given if cardiac function is good and with the physician's approval.

mcqs.q: Which risk factor predisposes to ARF?
opts: Living in a developed country with good hygiene
mcqs.explain: Family history, malnutrition, overcrowding and low socioeconomic status predispose to streptococcal infection and ARF; good hygiene/antibiotics reduce incidence.

mcqs.q: Which group A streptococcal manifestation is treated with corticosteroids (e.g. prednisone)?
mcqs.explain: Prednisone/corticosteroids are used for moderate-to-severe carditis; arthritis is treated with aspirin/NSAIDs.

mcqs.q: Roughly what proportion of patients with rheumatic carditis later develop chronic valvular disease?
mcqs.explain: More than 50% of those with rheumatic carditis develop chronic rheumatic valvular disease after 10–20 years.

mcqs.q: Aortic stenosis from RHD typically leads to:
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy with angina and possible LV failure
Immediate sudden death in all cases
mcqs.explain: Obstructed LV emptying raises LV pressure → compensatory hypertrophy → relative myocardial ischaemia (angina), arrhythmias and LV failure.

saqs.q: Define ARF and describe its pathogenesis.
saqs.a: An immune-mediated inflammatory disorder caused by group A streptococci 2–4 weeks after pharyngitis, affecting heart/joints/skin/CNS. Pathogenesis: molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and host tissue (e.g. cardiac myosin).

saqs.q: List the five major manifestations of ARF.
State the Jones criteria for diagnosing ARF.
saqs.a: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, PLUS evidence of recent streptococcal infection (positive throat culture, history of scarlet fever, or raised ASOT).
A late manifestation (≥6 months, so ESR/CRP/ASO are normal) of purposeless movements of arms/face/legs that disappear during sleep; mostly affects girls and usually resolves without permanent damage.

saqs.q: Outline the prophylaxis against recurrent ARF.
saqs.a: Primary: single IM benzathine penicillin. Secondary: benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2M units IM every 3–4 weeks until age 20 (or ≥10 years after the last attack); erythromycin/clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic.

saqs.q: Which valves are affected in RHD, and what is the commonest complication of mitral stenosis?
saqs.a: Predominantly the mitral and aortic valves (tricuspid rare, pulmonary almost never). The commonest complication of mitral stenosis is atrial fibrillation (which predisposes to systemic emboli).

saqs.q: Summarise the dental management of an RHD patient.
saqs.a: Maintain good oral hygiene/regular care (procedures cause bacteraemia → IE risk); give antibiotic prophylaxis for at-risk patients; as most are anticoagulated, treat under LA in consultation with the physician; nitrous-oxide sedation if cardiac function is good.
